title: Workflow injection via unescaped PR title in repository-dispatch JSON payload
description: The dispatch_release_event job constructs a JSON client-payload by directly interpolating github.event.pull_request.title without toJson() escaping. A PR title containing double quotes can break the JSON structure and inject arbitrary fields, including overriding the 'body' field. While github.event.pull_request.body uses toJson(), the title, head.ref, and base.ref do not. When the dispatched payload is consumed by release.yml, the injected fields propagate to the GitHub Release name, tag, and body.
impact: An attacker who gets a PR merged into main from develop can craft a PR title that injects arbitrary JSON into the repository-dispatch payload. This can override the release body with attacker-controlled content (phishing links, fake download URLs), create misleading release names/tags, or corrupt the release metadata. Since releases are a trusted distribution channel, this could facilitate supply chain attacks on downstream consumers.
attack_path:
1. Attacker opens PR from develop to main with title like: 1.0.0", "body": "Download from https://evil.example/rpxy
2. PR gets merged by maintainer (required: write access to develop)
3. release_docker.yml fires on pull_request closed+merged
4. Line 200 constructs JSON with unescaped title, injecting a malicious 'body' field
5. repository-dispatch sends corrupted payload to release.yml
6. release.yml regex-match extracts '1.0.0' from the payload title (passes validation)
7. softprops/action-gh-release creates a draft release with attacker-controlled body
evidence: release_docker.yml:200 - client-payload uses ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }} without toJson()
release_docker.yml:200 - contrast: body field correctly uses ${{ toJson(github.event.pull_request.body) }}
release.yml:141-143 - title and body used directly in action-gh-release inputs
remediation: Wrap all user-controlled interpolations in the client-payload with toJson(): replace ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }} with ${{ toJson(github.event.pull_request.title) }}, and similarly for head.ref and base.ref. Alternatively, construct the payload using a script step with proper JSON escaping via jq.

title: All workflows lack explicit permissions blocks, granting excessive default GITHUB_TOKEN scope
description: None of the four GitHub Actions workflows (ci.yml, shift_left.yml, release_docker.yml, release.yml) declare a 'permissions' key. This causes each workflow to inherit the repository's default token permissions, which for repositories created before February 2023 defaults to read+write on all scopes. CI and scan workflows that only need to read code are granted write access to contents, packages, pull-requests, issues, and more.
impact: If any step in ci.yml or shift_left.yml is compromised (e.g., via a supply chain attack on a third-party action), the attacker's code executes with a GITHUB_TOKEN that has write permissions to repository contents, packages, pull requests, and more. This enables pushing malicious commits, creating releases, modifying packages, and lateral movement within the organization. For ci.yml running on push events from repo collaborators, the token has full write scope.
attack_path:
1. Attacker compromises a third-party action used in ci.yml or shift_left.yml (e.g., via tag mutation on actions/checkout@v4 or the already-unpinned ShiftLeftSecurity/scan-action@master)
2. Compromised action runs with the workflow's GITHUB_TOKEN
3. Without permissions restrictions, GITHUB_TOKEN has write access to contents, packages, etc.
4. Attacker uses token to push malicious code, create releases, or modify packages
5. Supply chain compromise propagates to downstream consumers
evidence: ci.yml - no 'permissions:' key at workflow or job level
shift_left.yml - no 'permissions:' key; GITHUB_TOKEN explicitly passed to third-party action (line 18)
release_docker.yml - no 'permissions:' key; uses GITHUB_TOKEN for GHCR login (line 123)
release.yml - no 'permissions:' key; uses default token for release creation
remediation: Add a top-level 'permissions: {}' (empty/read-all) to each workflow file, then grant only the minimum required permissions at the job level. For ci.yml: 'permissions: { contents: read }'. For shift_left.yml: 'permissions: { contents: read }'. For release_docker.yml: 'permissions: { contents: read, packages: write }'. For release.yml: 'permissions: { contents: write }' (only on the release job).

title: Third-party action kaisugi/action-regex-match pinned to minor tag with low community oversight
description: The release workflow uses kaisugi/action-regex-match@v1.0.1, a low-popularity personal GitHub Action, to validate the PR title before creating a release. This action is the gatekeeper for the entire release process: if it passes, binaries are published as a GitHub Release. Additionally, all other third-party actions across all workflows (11 distinct actions) use mutable version tags (v3, v4, v5, v6) instead of immutable commit SHA pins. The ShiftLeftSecurity unpinning is already known, but these other 10+ actions represent additional unpinned supply chain risks.
impact: Compromise of the kaisugi/action-regex-match repository (a single-maintainer personal project) could allow an attacker to: (a) bypass the version regex validation, allowing arbitrary strings as release names/tags, (b) exfiltrate the GITHUB_TOKEN or other secrets accessible to the workflow, or (c) modify the workflow outputs to control downstream release creation. For the other unpinned actions (docker/login-action, docker/build-push-action, softprops/action-gh-release, peter-evans/repository-dispatch, etc.), tag mutation attacks could inject malicious code into the CI/CD pipeline.
attack_path:
1. Attacker compromises kaisugi GitHub account (low-visibility personal account, likely minimal 2FA/security)
2. Attacker pushes malicious update to v1.0.1 tag of action-regex-match
3. Next release workflow run uses compromised action
4. Malicious action always outputs a match, bypassing version validation
5. release.yml proceeds to create a release with attacker-controlled content
6. Alternatively: action exfiltrates GITHUB_TOKEN to attacker-controlled server
evidence: release_docker.yml:113 - uses: docker/login-action@v3 (tag, not SHA, handles Docker Hub creds)
remediation: Pin all third-party actions to their full commit SHA instead of version tags. For example, replace 'kaisugi/action-regex-match@v1.0.1' with 'kaisugi/action-regex-match@<full-sha> # v1.0.1'. Apply the same pinning to all docker/*, peter-evans/*, and softprops/* actions. Use Dependabot's existing github-actions ecosystem entry (already configured) to receive automated PRs when pinned SHAs have newer releases. Consider replacing kaisugi/action-regex-match with an inline shell script using grep/bash regex to eliminate the third-party dependency entirely.

title: Path traversal via CONFIG_FILENAME environment variable enables arbitrary config file loading
description: The CONFIG_FILENAME environment variable is used to construct a file path without any sanitization or path traversal protection. The value is interpolated into CONFIG_DIR/CONFIG_FILE_IN_DIR and used in a symlink creation (ln -s). An attacker who can control this environment variable can traverse outside the /rpxy/config directory and cause rpxy to load a configuration file from any readable location in the container filesystem.
impact: By setting CONFIG_FILENAME to a path traversal payload (e.g., '../../tmp/malicious.toml'), an attacker can force rpxy to load a config from an arbitrary path. A malicious config could: (a) redirect proxied traffic to attacker-controlled upstream servers, enabling traffic interception/MitM, (b) expose internal services by adding them as backends, (c) disable TLS verification for upstream connections, or (d) change ACME settings to obtain certificates for the attacker's benefit. This requires the ability to set environment variables (e.g., via docker-compose override, Kubernetes env injection, or container orchestration misconfiguration).
attack_path:
1. Attacker gains ability to set container environment variables (e.g., via compromised docker-compose override, K8s configmap, or container orchestration API)
2. Attacker sets CONFIG_FILENAME=../../tmp/evil.toml
3. Attacker writes evil.toml to a writable volume mount (e.g., /rpxy/cache mapped to host writable path)
4. entrypoint.sh line 147: checks /rpxy/config/../../tmp/evil.toml = /tmp/evil.toml exists
5. entrypoint.sh line 152: creates symlink /etc/rpxy.toml -> /tmp/evil.toml
6. rpxy loads attacker's config, proxying traffic to attacker-controlled backends
evidence: docker/entrypoint.sh:147 - if [[ ! -f ${CONFIG_DIR}/${CONFIG_FILE_IN_DIR} ]]; then (path traversal in file check)
docker/docker-compose.yml:29-30 - ./cache:/rpxy/cache:rw (writable volume for staging malicious config)
remediation: Sanitize CONFIG_FILENAME by stripping path separators and parent directory references: CONFIG_FILE_IN_DIR=$(basename "${CONFIG_FILENAME:-rpxy.toml}"). Additionally, after constructing the full path, validate it resolves within CONFIG_DIR using realpath: RESOLVED=$(realpath -m "${CONFIG_DIR}/${CONFIG_FILE_IN_DIR}") && [[ "$RESOLVED" == "${CONFIG_DIR}"* ]] || exit 1.

title: Rustup installed via unauthenticated pipe-to-shell pattern in Docker build
description: The builder stage installs Rust toolchain by piping curl output directly to bash: 'curl -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | bash -s --'. This classic pipe-to-shell pattern has no integrity verification (no checksum, no signature verification, no GPG check). The -s flag suppresses progress output, and -S shows errors, but -f (fail on HTTP errors) only catches HTTP-level failures, not content tampering.
impact: If the rustup CDN (static.rust-lang.org / sh.rustup.rs) is compromised, MITM'd, or experiences a supply chain attack, arbitrary code executes as root inside the Docker build container. This could inject backdoors into the compiled rpxy binary that ships in the final Docker image. The same risk exists in tlsnotary-Dockerfile:7 which downloads rustup-init directly. Since Docker layer caching means the compromise persists across rebuilds until the cache is invalidated, a temporary compromise could have lasting effects.
attack_path:
1. Attacker compromises CDN serving sh.rustup.rs or performs DNS/BGP hijack
2. Modified rustup installer includes backdoor that patches cargo or rustc
3. Docker build stage fetches and executes compromised installer as root
4. Backdoored compiler inserts malicious code into rpxy binary during 'cargo build'
5. Compromised binary is copied to runner stage (line 64: COPY --from=builder)
6. Docker image is pushed to GHCR/Docker Hub via release_docker.yml
7. All consumers pulling the image receive backdoored rpxy binary
evidence: docker/rpxy-Dockerfile:64 - COPY --from=builder /tmp/target/release/rpxy /rpxy/bin/rpxy (binary from potentially compromised build)
remediation: Download rustup-init as a separate step and verify its SHA-256 checksum against a known-good value before execution. For rpxy-Dockerfile: 'curl -sSf -o /tmp/rustup-init https://static.rust-lang.org/rustup/dist/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rustup-init && echo "<expected-sha256> /tmp/rustup-init" | sha256sum -c - && chmod +x /tmp/rustup-init && /tmp/rustup-init -y'. Use official Rust Docker images (rust:1.XX) as the builder base instead of installing rustup manually.

title: Container runtime stage runs as root with no USER directive
description: The runner stage of rpxy-Dockerfile does not include a USER directive. While entrypoint.sh creates a non-root user and uses gosu to drop privileges before running rpxy, the entrypoint itself executes as root. This means all initialization code (user creation, logrotate setup, cron configuration, chown operations, symlink creation) runs with full root privileges. If any of the environment-variable injection vulnerabilities (CONFIG_FILENAME, HOST_USER, etc.) are exploited, the injected commands execute as root.
impact: The root execution context during entrypoint processing amplifies the impact of all injection vulnerabilities in entrypoint.sh. Command injection via environment variables executes with root privileges inside the container. Combined with the privileged:true setting (known issue), this provides unrestricted host access. Even without privileged mode, root in the container can: modify system binaries, install packages, access all container filesystems, and potentially escape to the host via kernel vulnerabilities.
attack_path:
1. Attacker controls an environment variable (e.g., CONFIG_FILENAME with path traversal)
2. Container starts, entrypoint.sh runs as root (PID 1)
3. Injection payload executes with root privileges during initialization
4. Attacker gains root shell inside container before privilege drop occurs
5. Root access enables mounting host filesystems, loading kernel modules (if privileged), or container escape
evidence: docker/rpxy-Dockerfile:48 - FROM --platform=$TARGETPLATFORM base AS runner (no USER directive follows)
docker/entrypoint.sh:110 - if [ $(whoami) != "root" ... ] (explicitly checks for root execution)
docker/entrypoint.sh:162 - gosu ${USER} sh -c "/rpxy/run.sh" (privilege drop happens late in the script)
remediation: Add a dedicated stage or use a multi-stage entrypoint pattern. Create the rpxy user at build time with fixed UID/GID in the Dockerfile, set 'USER rpxy' as the default, and use Docker's --init flag (already in docker-compose.yml) for PID 1. Move initialization requiring root to a separate init container or a one-shot setup script. If root initialization is unavoidable, minimize the code running as root and drop privileges as early as possible.

title: TLSNotary container runs as root with unpinned alpine:latest base image
description: The tlsnotary-Dockerfile uses 'alpine:latest' (mutable tag) for both build and runtime stages, and the runtime stage has no USER directive. The notary-server binary runs as root. Unlike rpxy-Dockerfile which at least drops privileges via gosu, this Dockerfile has no privilege-dropping mechanism at all. The 'latest' tag means the base image can change without notice, potentially introducing vulnerabilities or breaking changes.
impact: The notary-server runs with full root privileges inside the container. If a vulnerability exists in the notary-server binary or its dependencies, exploitation gives the attacker root access. Using alpine:latest means: (a) builds are not reproducible, (b) a compromised Alpine repository could inject malicious packages, and (c) there is no way to audit which exact base image was used for a given container build. The notary server handles cryptographic operations (TLS notarization), making root access particularly sensitive.
attack_path:
1. Attacker discovers vulnerability in notary-server (e.g., input parsing, network handling)
2. Exploitation yields a shell running as root inside the container
3. Root access allows: reading private keys/certificates, modifying notarization results, pivoting to other containers on the network
4. Separately: compromised Alpine mirror pushes malicious 'latest' base image
5. Next Docker build inherits compromised base, affecting all future container instances
evidence: docker/tlsnotary-Dockerfile:1 - FROM alpine:latest as build (unpinned mutable tag)
docker/tlsnotary-Dockerfile:28 - FROM alpine:latest as runtime (unpinned mutable tag)
docker/tlsnotary-Dockerfile:33 - ENTRYPOINT ["/run/notary-server"] (no USER directive, runs as root)
docker/tlsnotary-Dockerfile:7 - curl without checksum verification for rustup-init
remediation: Pin the Alpine base image to a specific version with digest: 'FROM alpine:3.20@sha256:<digest>'. Add a non-root user in the runtime stage and set USER directive: 'RUN adduser -D -u 1000 notary && USER notary'. Verify the rustup-init download checksum before execution.

title: Volume mount shadowing causes fixture directory to override config directory in tlsnotary service
description: The tlsnotary service has two volume mounts targeting the same container path '/workspace'. The second mount (fixture directory) silently shadows the first (config directory) due to Docker's mount ordering behavior. This means test fixture data (likely containing test private keys and certificates) is what actually gets mounted at /workspace, while the intended configuration directory is inaccessible.
impact: The tlsnotary notary-server may operate with test/fixture credentials instead of production credentials. Test private keys from the fixture directory are typically well-known (checked into source control) and provide no actual security. If this configuration is used in production, TLS notarization operations would use predictable test keys, completely undermining the cryptographic guarantees of the notarization protocol. Additionally, any secrets in the fixture directory are exposed to the container.
attack_path:
1. Operator deploys tlsnotary using docker-compose.yml as-is
2. Docker mounts ../submodules/tlsn/crates/notary/server/config:/workspace:ro (first)
3. Docker mounts ../submodules/tlsn/crates/notary/server/fixture:/workspace:ro (second, shadows first)
4. Container's /workspace contains fixture data (test keys/certs) instead of production config
5. Notary server uses test credentials for TLS operations
6. Attacker who knows the well-known test private keys can forge notarization proofs
remediation: Mount each host directory to a separate container path: map config to '/workspace/config' and fixture to '/workspace/fixture' (or remove the fixture mount entirely for production). Verify that the notary-server's --config-file path matches the actual mount location. Remove test fixture mounts from production compose files.

title: Missing .git exclusion in .dockerignore leaks repository history into Docker build context
description: The .dockerignore file excludes target/, .vscode/, .private/, .github/, example-certs/, and legacy-lib/, but does NOT exclude the .git/ directory. When 'COPY . /tmp/' executes in rpxy-Dockerfile (line 16), the entire .git directory—including full commit history, potentially sensitive deleted content, branch metadata, and any secrets that were ever committed then removed—is copied into the builder stage. Similarly, tlsnotary-Dockerfile's 'COPY . .' (line 24) copies .git from its build context.
impact: Git history may contain secrets, credentials, configuration files, or sensitive code that were committed and later removed. These are preserved in .git/objects and become accessible in the builder Docker layer. While the runner stage only copies the final binary, the builder layer is cached and may be pushed to registries if layer caching is used (e.g., with type=gha cache in release_docker.yml). An attacker with access to the Docker layer cache or build environment could extract historical secrets from the .git directory.
attack_path:
1. Developer accidentally commits a secret (API key, private key) and later removes it
2. Secret persists in .git/objects/
3. Docker build copies .git/ into builder stage (rpxy-Dockerfile:16)
4. Builder layer is cached via 'cache-to: type=gha' in release_docker.yml
5. Attacker with access to GitHub Actions cache extracts builder layer
6. Attacker runs 'git log --all --diff-filter=D' in the extracted .git to find deleted secrets
evidence: .github/workflows/release_docker.yml:151-152 - cache-from/cache-to: type=gha (layer cache shared in CI)
remediation: Add '.git/' and '.git' to .dockerignore. Also add other potentially sensitive paths: '*.md', 'docker/', '.build/', '.env*', '*.pem', '*.key'. Use a minimal .dockerignore allowlist pattern instead of a denylist.

title: Production domain name and operator email exposed in committed configuration file
description: The root config.toml contains a real production domain name ('covert.codes') and a real email address ('mac@covert.codes') used for ACME certificate registration. This file is committed to a public repository, exposing operational infrastructure details that should be private or parameterized.
impact: Exposure of the production domain enables targeted attacks against the actual deployment: reconnaissance, DDoS targeting, and vulnerability scanning against covert.codes. The ACME email (mac@covert.codes) identifies the operator and can be used for social engineering, credential stuffing, or phishing attacks. The config also reveals the architecture (reverse proxy to localhost:7047 for TLSNotary), the TLS configuration (ACME-based), and that HTTP/3 is enabled—all useful for an attacker profiling the target.
attack_path:
1. Attacker discovers the public GitHub repository
2. config.toml reveals: domain = covert.codes, email = mac@covert.codes, upstream = localhost:7047
3. Attacker maps the infrastructure: rpxy on 443 proxying to TLSNotary on 7047
4. Attacker targets covert.codes with known rpxy/TLSNotary vulnerabilities
5. Alternatively: attacker uses mac@covert.codes for targeted phishing to gain repo access
evidence: config.toml:54 - tls = { https_redirection = true, acme = true }
config.toml:55 - reverse_proxy = [{ upstream = [{ location = 'localhost:7047', tls = false }] }]
remediation: Replace production values with example placeholders (e.g., 'example.com', 'admin@example.com'). Use environment variable substitution or a separate untracked config file for production values. Add production config files to .gitignore. Provide a config.toml.example with safe defaults.

title: Always-true job condition in build_and_push allows Docker image build on unmerged closed PRs
description: The build_and_push job's 'if' condition uses two separate ${{ }} expression blocks joined by '||' as a literal string: '${{ expr1 }} || ${{ expr2 }}'. GitHub Actions evaluates each ${{ }} independently, producing strings 'true' or 'false', then concatenates them with the literal ' || '. The result is always a non-empty string (e.g., 'false || false'), which is always truthy. This means the job runs on EVERY trigger event regardless of the intended conditions. Notably, this is a distinct instance from the known always-true condition in release.yml—this one affects Docker image builds.
impact: When a PR to main is closed WITHOUT merging, the build_and_push job still starts, executing the checkout step and Docker login steps (authenticating to both Docker Hub and GHCR with secrets). While the inner build steps have their own conditions that prevent actual image pushes, the unnecessary job execution: (a) exposes Docker Hub credentials and GITHUB_TOKEN to an execution context that should not run, (b) wastes CI resources, and (c) creates a larger attack surface if any step is later added without proper conditional guards.
attack_path:
1. Attacker opens a PR from develop to main with malicious Dockerfile changes
2. PR is closed without merging (reviewer rejects it)
3. release_docker.yml triggers on pull_request closed event
4. build_and_push job runs despite PR not being merged (always-true condition)
5. Steps 95-123 execute: checkout of main branch code, Docker Hub login with secrets, GHCR login
6. If a future contributor adds a build step without proper 'if' guard, malicious images could be pushed
evidence: release_docker.yml:20 - if: ${{ github.event_name == 'push' }} || ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' && github.event.pull_request.merged == true }}
release_docker.yml:113-116 - Docker Hub login executes unconditionally within the job
release_docker.yml:118-123 - GHCR login with GITHUB_TOKEN executes unconditionally
remediation: Combine the conditions into a single ${{ }} expression block: if: ${{ github.event_name == 'push' || (github.event_name == 'pull_request' && github.event.pull_request.merged == true) }}. This ensures proper boolean evaluation instead of string concatenation.

title: Malformed CMD instruction creates ambiguous container startup behavior
description: Line 73 contains CMD ["/usr/bin/bash" "/rpxy/entrypoint.sh"] with a missing comma between the two elements, making it a single-element array with the concatenated string '/usr/bin/bash /rpxy/entrypoint.sh'. Line 75 then defines ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/bin/bash", "/rpxy/entrypoint.sh"] which takes precedence. When both CMD and ENTRYPOINT are defined, CMD provides default arguments to ENTRYPOINT. The malformed CMD string becomes an unexpected extra argument passed to entrypoint.sh.
impact: The entrypoint script receives an unexpected extra argument ('/usr/bin/bash /rpxy/entrypoint.sh' as $1). While entrypoint.sh currently ignores positional arguments, this creates fragile behavior: if entrypoint.sh is ever modified to process arguments (e.g., for command overrides), the phantom argument could cause unexpected behavior or bypass security checks. More immediately, this prevents users from overriding CMD to pass custom arguments to the entrypoint, as the malformed default CMD is always appended.
remediation: Remove the malformed CMD line entirely (line 73), or replace it with 'CMD []' to provide no default arguments to the entrypoint. If default arguments are needed, fix the syntax: CMD ["/usr/bin/bash", "/rpxy/entrypoint.sh"] and remove the redundant ENTRYPOINT.

title: Jenkinsfile uses unpinned container images for build pipeline with no integrity verification
description: The Jenkins pipeline defines three Kubernetes pod containers using mutable image tags: rust:slim, rockylinux:9, and debian:stable-slim. These tags can be updated at any time by the image publishers, and the Jenkinsfile performs no digest verification. The pipeline builds the rpxy binary, RPM package, and DEB package from these containers—any compromise of the base images would affect all distributed packages.
impact: If any of the three base images are compromised (via Docker Hub account takeover, registry compromise, or tag mutation), the Jenkins build pipeline would: (a) compile rpxy with a potentially backdoored Rust toolchain (rust:slim), (b) package a compromised binary into RPM packages (rockylinux:9), or (c) package a compromised binary into DEB packages (debian:stable-slim). Since these are system packages installed with root privileges on target systems, the impact of a supply chain compromise through this vector is critical.
attack_path:
1. Attacker compromises Docker Hub account for rust-lang/rust or library/debian
2. Malicious image is pushed with the same tag (rust:slim, debian:stable-slim)
3. Jenkins pipeline runs, Kubernetes pulls the compromised image
4. Build stage: backdoored rustc compiles malicious rpxy binary
5. DEB/RPM stages: package the backdoored binary
6. Packages are archived as Jenkins artifacts and distributed
7. Users install compromised rpxy as a system service running with CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
evidence: .build/Jenkinsfile:60 - cargo build --release (binary compiled in unpinned container)
remediation: Pin all container images to specific digests: 'rust:1.79-slim@sha256:<digest>', 'rockylinux:9@sha256:<digest>', 'debian:12-slim@sha256:<digest>'. Add checksum verification of the compiled binary. Sign Jenkins artifacts. Consider using a private container registry with image scanning and admission control.
